epics.title: Cypher — the DeepSeek harness as a mind in the hive

features.title: DeepSeek Harness as a third hive harness
features.description:
dsh is our agent harness, forked from DeepSeek's developer preview at 47f9438 (MIT) and maintained independently at github.com/danielstewart77/dsh, checked out at /home/daniel/Storage/Dev/deepseek-harness. There is no upstream remote and nothing will be pulled from one: what they do with their copy from here on has no bearing on this code. A pristine clone of theirs can be kept separately for reading, and that is the only relationship. It is a pnpm/TypeScript monorepo of about fifty packages built on Cordis, where every capability — tools, providers, persistence, hooks, subagents — is a plugin composed from a profile's patch layers. The README calls it a developer preview and promises compatibility-breaking changes. Two surfaces ship: a web profile booting a browser UI on 3080, and a headless profile that creates one agent, submits the task, waits for quiescence, prints the last non-empty assistant message and exits. The profile templates are web and headless; there is no third.

Why it is worth the work: the hive already runs two harnesses behind one adapter seam, and the provider axis is orthogonal to the harness axis, so a third harness is a third template rather than a new architecture — provided the harness can do the things the seam assumes. Four of them dsh already does. It runs our hooks: the hooks-claude-code bridge reads an existing Claude Code hooks file and runs its command hooks on dsh's own typed interception points, mapping SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit with both additionalContext and deny, Stop, SubagentStart and SubagentStop — precisely the set the memory capture, surface injection, prose reminder and rotation staging use — with payloads carrying a session id and a string transcript path, and twenty-three of Claude Code's thirty hook events unsupported, none of them ours. Skills are SKILL.md directories, with four discovery roots, so skills_sync gains a third installed root and its compare, copy and write-back logic is unchanged. Providers are declarative and OpenAI or Anthropic shaped, where a custom provider takes a lowercase id, a base URL, an api protocol, an api-key environment variable and a model list with optional discovery — so the inference proxy is a custom provider and nothing else, and runtime.yaml's provider field extends to dsh without inventing a concept. And AGENTS.md is already the convention, with their own CLAUDE.md a symlink to it, the same trick this repo uses. MCP, subagents including a Codex-driving one, sandbox policy, session persistence and an ACP server are all present.
features.requirements:
Gate zero is the resume module: nothing else can start until an outside process can continue a dsh conversation by id. This is not a nice-to-have — it is the hive's central invariant meeting a harness that does not satisfy it. The invariant: hive-comms mints the conversation id when the session row is written and every spawn is handed that id, with resume when a transcript exists and a session-id flag when it is the conversation's first process, and a mind handed no id raises rather than inventing one. That is what makes a Telegram turn and a browser-terminal turn the same conversation. What dsh offered: the resume capability is real in core and already exercised, since cold-resumed subagents depend on it — but no surface exposes it. The headless runner reads the default model, creates a fresh persisted agent and takes no session argument at all; the ACP server is documented fresh-sessions-only; and the web app resumes only through its own browser client over the API gateway, not through anything a mind_server spawn can call. So a dsh mind could answer exactly one turn with no way to be handed the turn after it, and every downstream feature — rotation, cross-surface pickup, late turns, carry-forward — is a statement about a conversation persisting across processes.

Three different things called a session, kept apart on purpose because conflating them is how this gets over-engineered: the app's nominated conversation, which is a property of the app being rebuilt and nothing to do with this; the mind's own conversation, minted by hive-comms when the session row is written and handed to every spawn, which every mind already works this way; and dsh's own persisted on-disk agent session, which the resume module exists only to make addressable by the one above it and which is not otherwise ours to redesign.

The other two gaps. No interactive CLI: the browser terminal is tmux hosting an interactive harness process and dsh ships none — the bundles are base, headless and web-app, and the TUI survives only in archived agent notes. Three ways out in ascending cost: dsh minds are chat-surface-only and the tile is disabled for them; the tile hosts dsh's own web UI in an iframe instead of xterm.js, trading our terminal for theirs and losing the tmux persistence model; or we build the interactive surface. The first is the right opening move, since a mind that cannot be resumed cannot host a terminal anyway. And the transcript is theirs: session persistence writes dsh events zstd-compressed by default, with runs of three or more consecutive same-block assistant chunk deltas collapsed into packed chunk rows, and a sqlite backend also exists. The hook bridge hands over a transcript path, but the Stop hook's transcript read and the pty voice tailer both parse Claude's schema and would need a dsh reader — and our tooling assumes plain JSONL it can tail, so setting compression to none in the profile patch makes the log readable at the cost of disk, which is the cheap answer for a first mind.

Smaller things to know before building: the hook bridge parses its config once at load and the config path is process-level, with no per-session hook config discovery yet, so one process means one hook config. SessionStart hooks run detached, so their context can miss the first request, and the payload omits the model, the agent type and the session title. A blocking Stop hook forces another step via steer, which does not bite because our Stop hook exits zero and detaches, but a future blocking Stop would behave differently here than under Claude Code. A hook's systemMessage and updatedInput are logged but not model-visible — the same trap as Claude Code's systemMessage, already a standing rule. And headless mounts no HTTP server and opens no listening port, which is the right shape for a per-turn adapter.
features.acceptance_criteria:
Steps one and two are done. The resume module is built, public and MIT at github.com/danielstewart77/dsh-headless-resumable, developed in place inside the dsh checkout as its own repository, with the only change to upstream's tree being one workspace line, and fourteen tests over the real SessionStore and AgentRegistry. Both halves gate zero asked for were already in dsh-agent — create takes the id it is handed and resume loads a persisted one — so the work was the surface rather than a fight with session identity, and the harness_sid fallback is not needed. The command-line proof ran on qwen35-131k through the inference proxy: a second process continued the first's conversation and answered from its history; a resume against an unknown id refused with NO_SUCH_SESSION and persisted nothing; no id was refused before an agent existed; and a file-reading turn reported one tool call emitted, answered and succeeded. Two build lessons went into the module's README: tsdown 0.22's default config loader is one nothing in upstream's lockfile installs, so the lib build fails before compiling unless the tsx loader is passed; and both faces must be built rather than just the host one, because the base bundle mounts the api gateway whose client face emits its entry point.

Step two: the adapter is merged as hive_mind PR #260 with 36 tests of its own and the full suite green. Three things the requirements got wrong and the reviewers caught, recorded because the mistakes are the reusable part. The conversation id is resume_sid rather than the session row's own id — the row's id is permanent and a rotation replaces the conversation under it, so a harness run under the row id resumes precisely the context a rotation exists to drop, and reports an id comms logs as a mismatch on every turn. A re-POST of the sessions route is ordinary rather than exceptional, because comms respawns mid-turn on its own restart since its process table is empty while the mind's running turn is not — and replacing the session's state dict clears the turn-bleed guard, after which two dsh processes numbering events from one loaded prefix make the session log unloadable, dsh refuses both resume and create, and the conversation is dead permanently. And the provider route name is the profile's rather than the mind's, because a YAML mapping key cannot be computed, so a spawn naming a route the profile does not declare fails the boot — runtime.yaml's provider selects which endpoint and credential of the env block fill that one route in, the way it selects codex's model-provider overrides, and the credential has to be translated to the name the profile resolves, since the proxy answers 401 without one and the provider refuses rather than falling back.

What remains before Cypher takes a turn: his mind folder and runtime.yaml, the container with the built harness tree bind-mounted, the hook bridge pointed at his hooks file, and a dsh transcript reader for the Stop hook. The skills and files console pages are not mounted for this harness, because it reads skills from a third directory skills_sync has not been taught, and a route reporting the wrong one is worse than no route.
features.qa_tests:
The adapter's requirements and their fifteen tests: a turn with no model is refused and no session is registered, breaking the moment a default is substituted; a turn with no conversation id is refused, breaking if the adapter mints one, which is what the codex adapter does today and this must not; the conversation's first turn creates under the gateway's id, asserted on the argv carrying the session-id flag with exactly that id; the second turn on that id continues it, asserted on the argv carrying resume with the same id, breaking if the adapter creates every turn; a turn on an id dsh already has persisted resumes it even if this process has never seen it, which is the mind-restart case, breaking if 'first turn' is decided by in-process state rather than by what is on disk; the process is spawned in its own process group and killed as one, asserted on start_new_session and on the kill signalling the group rather than the pid; the assistant text reaches the operator verbatim; a turn that produced no text reports what the model did instead of being empty; a failed turn carries dsh's own error code; a turn that completed having produced nothing is not reported as a failure, which is the pair to the above and breaks if no-text is folded into error; a process that exits with no report line is reported as failed, breaking if a crashed harness reads as a quiet successful empty turn; the stop reason is recorded verbatim, scripted as max-tokens and asserted to be that exact string rather than end_turn; the tool traffic reaches the turn record per outcome, with one executed, one unanswered and one failed call told apart; the model and provider come from the mind's own configuration with no default anywhere in the path; and a terminal attach is refused as unsupported, distinct from the answer meaning this mind holds no live terminal. The tenth requirement — a refusal is reported as a refusal on every path — gets no test of its own, because every refusal path it governs is already asserted and the standard says a constraint whose named behaviours are covered earns nothing further.

The only stub in those tests is the transport, because that is where the process stops being ours; the scripted stdout is the dsh process's own report line.

stories.title: Build the resume-capable headless surface
stories.description: DONE. A bundle patch plus a startup provider, sibling to the headless bundle, parsing its own flag family off the command line the way the web startup parses host and port. Public and MIT at github.com/danielstewart77/dsh-headless-resumable, developed in place inside the dsh checkout as its own repository, with one workspace line the only change to upstream's tree. Fourteen tests over the real SessionStore and AgentRegistry.
stories.requirements: Take a session id and continue that session, submitting the task as an ordinary user message through the same submit path the fresh runner uses so turn semantics, hooks and persistence are identical whether the turn is the first or the fiftieth. Take a session id for a conversation that does not exist yet and create it under that id — the half that existed nowhere in dsh. Refuse rather than substitute. And report the turn result structurally, with the session id, stop reason and error code as data rather than as an exit code.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Both halves were already in dsh-agent, so the work was the surface rather than a fight with session identity, and the harness_sid fallback is not needed.
stories.qa_tests: Seven tests over the real session store and agent registry: a second task on one id continues one conversation, breaking the moment the runner calls create where it should call resume; a session is created under an id the harness did not mint, breaking if the create path mints its own; asked to continue a session that is not there it refuses non-zero naming the id and persists nothing; a task with no session id is refused before an agent exists and before a model request goes out, with the same for no model named; a completed turn reports where it ran and why it stopped as data; a failed turn reports its error code distinctly from a turn that completed having achieved nothing; and the tool traffic is counted per outcome, with executed, unparseable and refused told apart — because a tally that cannot distinguish refused from unparseable cannot say whether the model or the harness is at fault, and that is the measurement the first several nights are entirely about.

stories.title: Prove the resume module from the command line
stories.description: DONE. Step one of the sequence, and the gate's manual proof. Ran on qwen35-131k through the inference proxy: a second process continued the first's conversation and answered from its history; a resume against an unknown id refused with NO_SUCH_SESSION and persisted nothing; no id was refused before an agent existed; and a file-reading turn reported one tool call emitted, answered and succeeded.
stories.requirements: Create a session under a supplied id, kill the process, continue that session in a second process, and read both turns back out of the transcript.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The two-process proof, which is the gate rather than a unit test — spawning processes to prove the same assertion twice is tedium, and the gate needs the manual proof anyway.
stories.qa_tests: Done by hand, as the gate required.

stories.title: Write minds/harness/dsh_cli.py
stories.description: DONE. Merged as hive_mind PR #260 with 36 tests and the full suite green. One tracked adapter per harness in the hive_mind repo alongside the Claude and Codex ones, since Cypher is containerized and that repo's minds share one adapter rather than a per-mind copy. Per-turn path: one headless process per turn, a send coroutine plus a session-id kill, the provider resolved from runtime.yaml through the provider registry, POSIX spawns with start_new_session and killpg. No pty spawn in the first version.
stories.requirements: Ten requirements: no model is refused; no conversation id is refused; the first turn creates under the gateway's id and every later turn continues it, decided by whether that session exists rather than by guessing; one process per turn in its own group; the assistant text reaches the operator and a turn with none reports what the model did; a failed turn carries dsh's error code and is told apart from one that achieved nothing; every turn records its stop reason verbatim, max-tokens included as the context ceiling measured rather than a crash to explain, and its tool traffic per outcome; the provider and model come from runtime.yaml with the proxy route itself in the profile's patch layer; chat surfaces only, with a terminal attach refused as unsupported rather than as a mind with no terminal; and a refusal is reported as a refusal on every path.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Three reviewer corrections recorded because the mistakes are the reusable part: the conversation id is resume_sid rather than the row id; a re-POST of the sessions route is ordinary rather than exceptional, and mishandling it kills the conversation permanently; and the provider route name is the profile's rather than the mind's.
stories.qa_tests: Fifteen tests, each importing the adapter and calling it, with only the transport stubbed. The max-tokens test asserts that exact string rather than end_turn. The mind-restart test is the one that catches 'first turn' being decided by in-process state rather than by disk.

stories.title: Create Cypher's mind folder and runtime.yaml
stories.description: Outstanding. Part of what remains before Cypher takes a turn.
stories.requirements: His own mind folder with DSH_HOME inside it, and a runtime.yaml naming his model and provider. The model is qwen35-131k through the inference proxy, metered against the mind's own key.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The adapter resolves his model and provider from his own file.
stories.qa_tests: A spawn carries the model and the provider route from his runtime.yaml with no default anywhere in the path. The provider route must be one the profile declares, since a YAML mapping key cannot be computed and a spawn naming an undeclared route fails the boot.

stories.title: Stand up Cypher's container with the harness tree bind-mounted
stories.description: Outstanding. Containerized, with the built harness tree bind-mounted in — the same pattern every other containerized mind uses for the hive repo it runs. The tree is not installable from npm and does not need to be: it is ours, built in place.
stories.requirements: The built tree mounted, not installed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The container runs the adapter against the built harness.
stories.qa_tests: A turn completes inside the container. Note that the mind folder and the playground are the only mounts — every other mind mounts the whole of Dev, and what this one cannot see is the point.

stories.title: Point the hook bridge at Cypher's hooks file
stories.description: Outstanding. Step three of the sequence: confirm the memory pipeline fires end to end. Note the bridge parses its config once at load and the config path is process-level, with no per-session hook config discovery yet — one process, one hook config.
stories.requirements: The bridge loaded and configured against a settings file in his DSH_HOME.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A hook fires on a turn and the memory pipeline completes.
stories.qa_tests: Verified by booting him and watching a hook fire — this is configuration rather than code. Watch for the systemMessage trap: a hook's systemMessage and updatedInput are logged but not model-visible, the same as under Claude Code.

stories.title: Write a dsh transcript reader for the Stop hook and the voice tailer
stories.description: Outstanding. Step four. Both parse Claude's schema today. The cheap first-mind answer is setting compression to none in the profile patch, which makes the log readable at the cost of disk, with a format shim.
stories.requirements: A reader for dsh's event schema, or compression off plus a shim for the first mind.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The Stop hook can read a dsh transcript.
stories.qa_tests: A real dsh session file is read correctly. The real files are multi-frame zstd — one frame per append — so a fixture compressed in one call would pass against a reader that decodes only the first frame, which on a real file yields the header line alone.

stories.title: Teach skills_sync the third installed root before mounting the console pages
stories.description: Outstanding. The skills and files console pages are deliberately not mounted for this harness, because it reads skills from a third directory skills_sync has not been taught, and a route reporting the wrong one is worse than no route.
stories.requirements: The third root added, then the pages mounted.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The console's skills table reports Cypher's actual skills.
stories.qa_tests: A skill installed in the dsh root is reported, and the five states are correct against it. Mounting the page before this would have it report confidently about the wrong directory.

stories.title: Decide the terminal question with a working mind in hand
stories.description: Step five. Three ways out in ascending cost: dsh minds are chat-surface-only with the tile disabled; the tile hosts dsh's own web UI in an iframe, trading our terminal for theirs and losing the tmux persistence model; or we build the interactive surface. The first is the right opening move. Note that Cypher has since got a tmux browser terminal with pane rotation, so this was decided in favour of building it.
stories.requirements: Decided with a working mind rather than in the abstract.
stories.qa_tests: The tile attaches and the pane rotates, which is how the decision reads now.

stories.title: Harden against other models' tool-call dialects
stories.description: A later pass. Alternate runs across models once the adapter is carrying real work. Cypher's model is qwen35-131k through the proxy.
stories.requirements: Driven by real failures across alternate runs rather than written speculatively.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A named model that fails a tool call succeeds after the hardening.
stories.qa_tests: Each hardening names the model that motivated it. A rule with no named failure behind it is speculative and does not belong.

stories.title: Keep lefthook out of the fork
stories.description: DONE, day one. lefthook, its config and the postinstall that installs it were removed. This host's git hooks path is a global secret guard, and lefthook's installer replaces the hook set wholesale — it had already silently clobbered pre-commit, pre-push and pre-merge-commit, leaving every repo on the machine unguarded until the secret guard was reinstalled.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An install of the fork does not touch the global hooks path.
stories.qa_tests: After a fresh install, the global secret guard is still in place. The window it was off — 2026-10-02 17:33 to 21:38 — is recorded, with the restore command.
